680.title: Shabads close
680.hook: births, weddings, deaths, days: the Granth sings through them all
680.howItsDone: Sikhs mark birth, marriage, illness, death and ordinary days with shabads, chiefly from the Guru Granth Sahib, sung by families, sangats and ragis, so the Guru's words are present at every turn of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, singing it for someone, and your line: sing it for them. Did you send a line of comfort to someone having a hard time? Today we close this whole stretch of shabads for a life, and look at it from end to end. Day six hundred eighty.

Picture a single family over one long life. A baby comes home, and a grandfather sings. Twenty-five years later, the same child walks four slow rounds around the Guru Granth Sahib. There are hospital nights, a move across an ocean, a new house blessed. And one day, the family gathers to sing for that same person one last time. Through all of it, someone is singing: mostly from the Guru Granth Sahib, sometimes from the Tenth Guru's own writings. For thirty-five days, this path has followed that life. Today: shabads close.
screen: `A BABY COMES HOME.` → `FOUR ROUNDS, A NEW HOUSE.` → `ONE LAST SONG.`

segments.voice: Look back at the turns we've walked. Birth: Guru Arjan's joy when his son Hargobind was born, a gift arriving. Marriage: the four laavan of Guru Ram Das, dharma, fearless, longing and union, and before them the palla placed in the bride's hand while the hem of the Lord is sung. Protection: the hot wind that doesn't touch, and the Guru's hand over your head. Neighbors: some say Ram, some Khuda, one Lord behind every name. Loss: the Tenth Guru's song to the beloved Friend from the forest, and Guru Nanak's laments, which open with blessed and remember that all must go. Courage: grant me this, never turn from good, and the death of the brave, accepted in His court. And then the ordinary days: a shabad for your home, the ragi choosing the right song, two lines learned by heart, a hymn sung for a friend. Two of those, the song to the Friend and grant me this, come from the Dasam Granth, the writings linked to the Tenth Guru; the rest are in the Guru Granth Sahib. Here's what that adds up to. The Guru Granth Sahib isn't only read on special occasions. It's built to meet every turn of a life. Sikhs say the Guru is present in the shabad, so at each turn, the Guru is there too: at the cradle, at the wedding, at the bedside, at the cremation. That's why a Sikh family doesn't need to invent words for the big moments. They're already written, and already sung. And you don't need to know all of them. A handful, really known, can carry a life.
screen: `BIRTH, MARRIAGE, PROTECTION.` · `NEIGHBORS, LOSS, COURAGE.` · `THE ORDINARY DAYS.` · `THE GURU AT EVERY TURN.` · then, large: `A HYMN FOR EVERY TURN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your five shabads. Sit, and go slowly through the turns of a life: a birth, a wedding, a hard night, a loss, an ordinary morning. For each one, let a line from this path come to mind, the one you'd want sung then. Don't worry about exact words; the meaning is enough. Count them on your fingers, one to five. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after the fifth. The bell holds the time.
Shabads close. Thirty-five days of hymns for a life: births, weddings, protection, loss, courage and ordinary days, the Granth singing through them all.
Your line: a hymn for every turn. Today, write down your five lines, one for each turn, and keep the list somewhere safe. Day six hundred eighty.

681.title: Sangrand, the new month
681.hook: the first day of each month, when the Barah Maha is read and people gather
681.howItsDone: On Sangrand, the first day of each Punjabi solar month, many gurdwaras hold a morning program where the month's stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha is read, with kirtan, Ardas and langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shabads close, and your line: a hymn for every turn. Did you write down your five lines? Now the year's last stretch begins: the calendar of the banis, the days of the year that Sikhs gather around. Day six hundred eighty-one.

The first of the month comes with its own small rituals. Rent is due, the gym is suddenly full, and the calendar on the fridge gets flipped to a new picture. It's a small fresh start that comes twelve times a year, whether you're ready or not. In many Sikh communities, the first day of the month has a name and a gathering of its own. Some who rarely make it to the gurdwara come early that morning. Today: Sangrand.
screen: `THE FIRST OF THE MONTH.` → `A SMALL FRESH START.` → `A GATHERING OF ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: Sangrand is the Punjabi form of sankranti: the day the sun moves into a new sign of the zodiac. In the traditional Punjabi calendar, that's when each solar month begins: Chet, Vaisakh, Jeth, and on through the year. You've met those months already. Earlier this year, we walked through the Barah Maha, the twelve months, Guru Arjan's song in Raag Majh, in which each month becomes a stage in the soul's longing for the Beloved. On Sangrand, many gurdwaras read that month's stanza aloud, so the sangat begins the month with its verse. In Chet, the Chet stanza. In Vaisakh, the Vaisakh stanza. Families come for kirtan, Ardas and langar. Now, a fair question: does the Granth say some days are holier than others? Guru Arjan answers it inside the Barah Maha itself. Near the end, on Ang one thirty-six, he says, in paraphrase: the months, the days, the moments are blessed for those on whom the Lord casts His glance of grace. So the date isn't magic. What makes a day good is remembering God in it. Sikhs hold that in different ways. Many love Sangrand as a chance to begin the month in sangat. Others, including some Sikh scholars and reformers, prefer not to make the date itself special, and say every day is the same before God. Both look to the same line. And both agree on what the line asks: whatever the date, begin it remembering.
screen: `SANKRANTI: THE SUN'S NEW SIGN.` · `THE MONTH'S STANZA, READ ALOUD.` · `GRACE MAKES THE DAY BLESSED.` · `BEGIN THE MONTH REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `THE MONTH BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark this month's Sangrand. Sit, and find out, or guess, which Punjabi month you're in right now. Think back over the past month: one thing to leave behind, one thing to carry forward. Then picture the first day of next month, and decide on one small way to begin it remembering: a line read, a visit, a quiet minute. If you pray, you can say Waheguru to open the new month. The bell holds the time.
Sangrand. The first day of a Punjabi solar month, when the sun enters a new sign, and many gurdwaras read that month's stanza of the Barah Maha.
Your line: the month begins. Today, look up the date of the next Sangrand and put it in your calendar with one line to read that morning. Day six hundred eighty-one.

682.title: Puranmashi, the full moon
682.hook: full-moon gatherings recall Guru Nanak's birth at the Katak full moon
682.howItsDone: Many gurdwaras hold a monthly Puranmashi diwan on the full moon, with kirtan, katha and langar; Guru Nanak's gurpurab is celebrated on the full moon of Katak.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sangrand, and your line: the month begins. Did you mark the next first-of-the-month in your calendar? The sun sets the Punjabi months. Today, the moon gets its turn. Day six hundred eighty-two.

Once a month it happens on the way to the car or out with the trash: the full moon, huge and low and orange over the rooftops. People stop. They take bad phone photos of it. They text someone, did you see the moon? Strangers on the same sidewalk point it out to each other. For a minute, the sky is the news. In Sikh communities, that night has a name, and in many places, a gathering. Today: Puranmashi.
screen: `ONCE A MONTH, PEOPLE LOOK UP.` → `BAD PHONE PHOTOS OF THE MOON.` → `A NIGHT WITH A NAME.`

segments.voice: Puranmashi means the full-moon day. Many gurdwaras hold a special diwan on the full moon each month, with kirtan, katha and langar, sometimes running late into the evening. Why the full moon? The reason Sikhs give is Guru Nanak. His birth, his gurpurab, is celebrated on the full moon of the month of Katak, in October or November. On that night, gurdwaras are lit up, processions fill the streets in the days before, and an unbroken reading of the Guru Granth Sahib often ends that morning. So each month's full moon carries a small echo of that one. Historians add a detail worth knowing. Some early accounts of Guru Nanak's life give his birth in the spring month of Vaisakh, not Katak. The Katak full moon is the long-standing tradition. The sources disagree, and Sikhs have kept the Katak celebration. The moon also shines inside the Granth. In Guru Nanak's Aarti, on Ang six sixty-three, the whole sky is pictured as a platter for worship, with the sun and the moon as its lamps. In paraphrase: the sky is the plate, the sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls. The full moon, in that picture, isn't a symbol of anything you have to explain. It's simply one of the lamps the universe holds up to its Creator, and you get to see it.
screen: `PURANMASHI: THE FULL MOON.` · `GURU NANAK'S KATAK FULL MOON.` · `SOURCES DIFFER ON THE DATE.` · `THE MOON AS A LAMP IN THE AARTI.` · then, large: `FULL MOON, FULL HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the moon. If it's night and you can see it, go to a window or step outside and look. If it's day, or cloudy, picture the last full moon you remember. Let it be a lamp held up in a huge silent room. Breathe slowly while you look. Think of how many people across the world are under the same moon tonight. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, as one more voice in that room. The bell holds the time.
Puranmashi. The full moon, when many gurdwaras gather, echoing Guru Nanak's gurpurab on the full moon of Katak.
Your line: full moon, full heart. Tonight or at the next full moon, look up for one minute and send the sight to someone you love. Day six hundred eighty-two.

683.title: The Nanakshahi calendar
683.hook: in 2003 the SGPC adopted a solar Sikh calendar, later revised; Sikhs still discuss which dates to keep
683.howItsDone: Sikh gurdwaras publish yearly calendars of gurpurabs; many follow the SGPC's revised Nanakshahi calendar, and some keep the original 2003 version, so dates can differ between communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Puranmashi, and your line: full moon, full heart. Did you look up and send the sight to someone? The sun gave us Sangrand, the moon gave us Puranmashi. Today: what happens when the two calendars disagree. Day six hundred eighty-three.

Is the party on the actual birthday, or the nearest Saturday? Your parents' house, or mine? Which date counts? Now stretch that question across a whole people spread across the world, with festivals set by the moon, the sun and the Western calendar all at once. A gurpurab set by the moon can move by weeks from one year to the next. Sikhs have tried to solve that. Today: the Nanakshahi calendar.
screen: `WHICH DATE COUNTS?` → `MOON, SUN AND THE WESTERN YEAR.` → `A GURPURAB THAT MOVES.`

segments.voice: For centuries, Sikh festivals followed the Bikrami calendar, the traditional Indian calendar used across North India. Its months follow the sun, but many holy days are set by the moon, so their dates shift each year. A Canadian Sikh, Pal Singh Purewal, proposed a new calendar: the Nanakshahi, named for Guru Nanak, its years counted from his birth in 1469. It uses a solar year that keeps pace with the Western one, so each month begins on the same date every year, and each gurpurab falls on a fixed day. Chet, the first month, begins in mid-March. In 2003, the SGPC, the body that manages the major gurdwaras in Punjab, adopted it. Its supporters, in Punjab and abroad, welcomed dates you could plan around, a calendar of the community's own. Others felt something precious was lost, the old link with the moon, and with how their grandparents had kept the days. Even in 2003, a few days, Guru Nanak's gurpurab among them, had stayed with the moon. In 2010, the SGPC revised the calendar and moved more gurpurabs back to lunar dates. Today, the SGPC's revised calendar is widely followed, and some gurdwaras, in Punjab and abroad, keep the original 2003 version. Sikhs still discuss it, sometimes with real feeling. Which dates to keep is a live question, and people of deep faith stand on different sides. What doesn't change is what the dates are for: to gather, to sing, and to remember the Gurus.
screen: `THE BIKRAMI: SUN AND MOON.` · `PUREWAL'S SOLAR NANAKSHAHI.` · `ADOPTED IN 2003, REVISED IN 2010.` · `DIFFERENT DATES, THE SAME PURPOSE.` · then, large: `DATES, DISCUSSED KINDLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: note one gurpurab date. Sit for a moment and think of one Guru you've come to know on this path. Picture how you'd want to remember their day: a shabad, langar, a quiet hour. After the bell, look up when their gurpurab falls this year, and if your local gurdwara keeps a different date, note both. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for the Guru you chose. The bell holds the time.
The Nanakshahi calendar. A solar Sikh calendar counted from Guru Nanak's birth, adopted by the SGPC in 2003 and revised in 2010, and still discussed among Sikhs.
Your line: dates, discussed kindly. Today, if a disagreement about a date or a plan comes up, keep in mind what the day is for, and say it gently. Day six hundred eighty-three.

684.title: Guru Ram Das's gurpurab
684.hook: his birth is marked in autumn with kirtan at Amritsar, the city he began
684.howItsDone: On Guru Ram Das's gurpurab in autumn, the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is illuminated, kirtan continues through the day, and many pilgrims bathe in the sarovar he began.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nanakshahi calendar, and your line: dates, discussed kindly. Did you look up a gurpurab date? Now the calendar fills with faces. For the next six days, one Guru's day at a time. Day six hundred eighty-four.

Some people are remembered for what they said. Some for what they built. And a few are remembered for a place so alive that it's hard to imagine the world without it. Stand at the edge of the pool in Amritsar at two in the morning: the Harmandir Sahib glowing gold on the water, kirtan floating across, people walking the marble barefoot in the cool air. It all began with one man, a pool, and a lot of digging. Today: Guru Ram Das's gurpurab.
screen: `REMEMBERED FOR A PLACE.` → `AMRITSAR AT TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `ONE MAN, A POOL, A LOT OF DIGGING.`

segments.voice: Guru Ram Das was born in Lahore and named Jetha. Tradition remembers him as an orphan who sold boiled grain on the street to get by. He came to Goindval, served in the langar of the third Guru, Guru Amar Das, married his daughter, Bibi Bhani, and became the fourth Guru. You've met him already on this path: he wrote the four laavan. His great work of building began with a pool. He had a sarovar, a sacred pool, dug out, and a town grew around it. It was called Ramdaspur, Guru Ram Das's town, and later Amritsar, the pool of nectar. Tradition says he invited traders and craftspeople to settle there, and the town became a center of Sikh life. His son Guru Arjan completed the pool and built the Harmandir Sahib in the middle of it. Guru Arjan wrote, on Ang six twenty-five, in paraphrase: bathing in the pool of Ram Das, all the sins one has committed are washed away. Sikhs read that bathing as both outward and inward: the water, and the Name. His gurpurab falls in the autumn, and on that day Amritsar is full. The Harmandir Sahib is lit, kirtan goes on through the day, and many come to bathe in the pool he began. Sikhs often speak of him with a particular tenderness: the humble one, whose door is open to all. A city, a pool and a wedding song: that's quite a legacy for a boy who once sold grain.
screen: `JETHA, A BOY FROM LAHORE.` · `A POOL DUG, A TOWN GROWN.` · `RAMDASPUR BECOMES AMRITSAR.` · `THE POOL WASHES WITHIN.` · then, large: `THE CITY OF THE POOL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the pool at night. Close your eyes. See the dark water, still, with a golden building in its center and its reflection beneath. Hear the kirtan carried over the water. Picture people walking slowly around the edge, barefoot on cool marble. Let your breath slow to their pace. If you've been there, remember it; if not, let it be new. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you walk the edge in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Guru Ram Das's gurpurab. The fourth Guru's birthday, marked in autumn with kirtan and light at Amritsar, the city that grew around the pool he began.
Your line: the city of the pool. Today, notice one place that began because someone started digging, and give thanks for whoever did. Day six hundred eighty-four.

685.title: Guru Angad's gurpurab
685.hook: his birth is remembered with Gurmukhi and the langar of Mata Khivi
685.howItsDone: On Guru Angad's gurpurab in spring, gurdwaras hold kirtan and langar, and some hold Gurmukhi classes, remembering the script he spread and Mata Khivi's kitchen at Khadur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Ram Das's gurpurab, and your line: the city of the pool. Did you give thanks for someone who started digging? Today, the second Guru, and the woman beside him. Day six hundred eighty-five.

Two things in Sikh life touch almost everyone, every day, and you barely notice them. One is the shape of the letters: every gutka, the street signs of Indian Punjab, every line of scripture on your phone in Gurmukhi. The other is the free kitchen: a hot plate of dal and roti, served to anyone who sits down on the floor. A script and a kitchen. Sikh memory ties both, in a special way, to one couple in a village called Khadur. Today: Guru Angad's gurpurab.
screen: `THE SHAPE OF THE LETTERS.` → `A HOT PLATE ON THE FLOOR.` → `ONE COUPLE IN KHADUR.`

segments.voice: Guru Angad was born in 1504 and named Lehna. He was a devotee of the goddess Durga, tradition says, until he heard a Sikh reciting Guru Nanak's hymns, and went to find the Guru at Kartarpur. He served him so completely that Guru Nanak named him his successor and gave him a new name: Angad, from ang, a limb, part of the Guru's own body. You heard it from Satta and Balvand a couple of weeks ago: same light, new body. As Guru, he settled at Khadur, and two things grew there. The first is Gurmukhi. Tradition credits Guru Angad with shaping and spreading the script the Guru's words are written in, so that ordinary people, not only scholars, could read them. Historians discuss how much of the script existed before him, but Sikhs remember him as the one who put it in children's hands. The second is the langar, and here the credit goes to his wife, Mata Khivi. She ran the kitchen at Khadur, feeding everyone who came. Satta and Balvand praise her in their var, on Ang nine sixty-seven. In paraphrase: Khivi, a good woman, gives shade like a leafy tree; she serves rice pudding rich with ghee. Sikhs remember her as the mother of the langar. His gurpurab falls in spring. Many gurdwaras mark it with kirtan, and some with Gurmukhi classes for children, and of course the kitchen is open.
screen: `LEHNA BECOMES ANGAD.` · `GURMUKHI: THE SCRIPT FOR ALL.` · `MATA KHIVI'S KITCHEN.` · `PRAISED IN THE GRANTH.` · then, large: `THE SCRIPT AND THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one Gurmukhi letter. Find a pen and paper, or use your finger on the table. The first letter of the Gurmukhi alphabet is oorhaa; if you can, look at it on your screen, then draw it slowly, once, then again. If you can't see it, draw the first letter of your own name with the same care. Don't worry if it's wobbly; every child's first one is. As you draw, think of everyone who learned to read the Guru's words from that letter. If you pray, you can say Waheguru when you finish. The bell holds the time.
Guru Angad's gurpurab. The second Guru's birthday, remembered with Gurmukhi, the script he spread, and the langar of Mata Khivi at Khadur.
Your line: the script and the kitchen. Today, teach someone one thing, or feed someone one thing, and do it the way Khadur did: freely. Day six hundred eighty-five.

686.title: Guru Amar Das's gurpurab
686.hook: remembered at Goindval, the well of eighty-four steps
686.howItsDone: On Guru Amar Das's gurpurab, gurdwaras hold kirtan and langar, and at Goindval Sahib some pilgrims descend the baoli, reciting Japji Sahib on each of its eighty-four steps.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Angad's gurpurab, and your line: the script and the kitchen. It ends a week that closed the shabads for a life, began the month at Sangrand, looked up at the full moon, talked kindly about dates, and visited the city of the pool. Today, a well. Day six hundred eighty-six.
screen: `A HYMN FOR EVERY TURN · THE MONTH BEGINS · FULL MOON · DATES · THE POOL · THE SCRIPT AND THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Here's a life that runs the other way from the usual story of starting young. Tradition remembers a man who spent most of his life as a devout pilgrim of his own tradition, walking to the Ganges again and again. Then, already old, he hears a young woman singing Guru Nanak's hymns while she churns butter, and everything changes. Years later, past seventy, tradition says, he becomes the third Guru. Today: Guru Amar Das's gurpurab.
screen: `A LIFE THAT STARTS LATE.` → `A LIFETIME A PILGRIM.` → `A SONG AT THE BUTTER CHURN.`

segments.voice: The young woman singing at the churn was Bibi Amro, Guru Angad's daughter, married into his family. Tradition says he was so moved that he went to Khadur, and for years served Guru Angad: carrying water from the river before dawn, every day. He became Guru, tradition says, past seventy. He settled at Goindval, on the river Beas, and two things there are remembered on his gurpurab. The first is the langar. Tradition says he asked everyone who came to eat in the free kitchen first, sitting together on the floor, before meeting him: high caste and low, rich and poor, side by side. Sikhs remember a saying linked to him: first the pangat, the row of people eating, then the sangat, the gathering. The second is the baoli, a stepwell. He had a deep well built at Goindval, with steps leading down to the water: eighty-four of them. Water open to everyone, with no caste rule at the bottom. Today some pilgrims walk down to the water reciting the Japji Sahib once on each step, a long, slow devotion. Some Sikhs connect the eighty-four steps to the old Indian idea of eighty-four lakh lives; others keep it simply as a practice of patience, and some point out that Gurbani speaks of liberation by grace and the Name, not by counting. Either way, it's a picture of the third Guru himself: going down, step by step, slowly, toward water.
screen: `A PILGRIM, AND A SONG AT THE CHURN.` · `PANGAT FIRST, THEN SANGAT.` · `THE BAOLI AT GOINDVAL.` · `ONE JAPJI ON EACH STEP.` · then, large: `EIGHTY-FOUR STEPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drink water slowly. Pour a glass of water and sit with it. Look at it first. Think of the people at Goindval, walking down eighty-four steps to reach it. Then drink, in small sips, slowly, noticing the cool of it, the way it goes down. Between sips, breathe. Let the glass take the whole length of the bell if it can. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each sip. The bell holds the time.
Guru Amar Das's gurpurab. The third Guru's birthday, remembered at Goindval: the langar where all sat together, and the well of eighty-four steps.
Your line: eighty-four steps. Today, take one task you've been rushing and go down into it slowly, one step at a time. Day six hundred eighty-six.
